taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO as Opuntia macrorhiza Engelm. Older infraspecific combinations are synonyms; do not split them into separate learner concepts.
look_here_first: Compare the whole plant against Texas pricklypear before counting spines. O. macrorhiza is usually a low, sprawling grassland cactus with smaller pads close to the ground. Then check the areoles: relatively few permanent spines, often with the main spine strongly bent or deflexed near its base, plus orange-brown glochids.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — Purola Preserve north Hays County natural-flora list includes Opuntia macrorhiza as naturally occurring. Travis — UT Plant Resources Center Travis County Cactaceae specimen index includes O. macrorhiza. Williamson — UT PRC Vascular Plants of Williamson County provides a detailed local treatment.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Exact target-zone county documentation only. This species remains separate from O. engelmannii var. lindheimeri; use comparative morphology rather than pad presence alone.

best_field_traits: low sprawling or radiating succulent shrub, often close to the ground
flattened photosynthetic cladodes/pads commonly smaller than the large Texas-pricklypear anchor
true cactus areoles repeated over the pads
areoles with brown wool and dense orange to brown glochids
permanent spines commonly few; main spine often strongly bent at the base and deflexed
large showy flowers yellow with reddish or rose-red pigmentation toward the petal bases in the detailed Williamson treatment
inferior ovary with areoles on the surrounding pericarpel tissue
morphology_keys.habit: Often forms a low radial plant with branches/pads touching the ground rather than a taller shrubby pricklypear.
morphology_keys.areole: Areoles are the family-defining structure; in this species the wool/glochids and few bent permanent spines are useful comparison characters.
morphology_keys.spines: The strongest permanent spine is often bent sharply near its base and angles downward. Do not use spine count alone.
morphology_keys.flower: Large radial flowers with many free perianth segments and numerous stamens; local treatment describes yellow inner segments with rose-red color toward the base.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Against O. engelmannii var. lindheimeri, use overall low habit, smaller pad proportions, areole spacing, glochid color, and the bent/deflexed main spine as a character suite—not a single feature.

comparisons.key_distinctions: O. macrorhiza is generally lower and more sprawling than the common Texas pricklypear anchor, with smaller pads and a characteristic tendency for a few strongly bent/deflexed permanent spines. Confirm with multiple traits because Opuntia spine number is variable.
